data.html:
Lesson Overview

In your last lesson, you built your mousetrap car's power system and axles — transferring spring energy into wheel motion. Now it's time to ask a harder question: how well does everything work together? This lesson moves into the Creationeering™ phase of Performance. You'll focus on component alignment and quality, learning how to spot problems like wobbly wheels or bent axles, and how to fix them so your car moves with precision and efficiency. Small improvements in alignment and quality can make a huge difference in how far and how fast your car travels.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Explain why component alignment matters for optimal performance in an engineered system.
  • Identify common quality issues in mousetrap car components, such as bent axles or rough wheel edges.
  • Apply practical techniques to improve the alignment and quality of your car's power system, axles, and wheels.
  • Analyze how component quality and alignment affect your car's overall speed and distance.
  • Connect careful craftsmanship in engineering to our responsibility to steward God's creation wisely.

data.html:
Genesis 1:31 (KJV): "And God saw every thing that He had made, and, behold, it was very good."

God didn't just call His creation good — He called it very good. Every component, from the smallest cell to the largest galaxy, was perfectly arranged and working exactly as intended. That's the standard of quality we're aiming for in engineering: not just something that works, but something that works

Craftsmanship as Stewardship

Think about the human body for a moment. Your knee joint doesn't just sort of line up with your leg bones — it aligns with incredible precision so that you can walk, run, and jump without your body falling apart. If that alignment were even slightly off, every step would create extra friction, wear, and eventually pain. God built the universe with that same attention to detail, and as engineers, we're called to imitate that care.

Stewardship means managing what God has given us responsibly. That includes the materials, time, and tools you're using to build your mousetrap car. Rushing through assembly or ignoring a wobbly wheel isn't just bad engineering — it's a missed opportunity to do your best work. Excellence in craftsmanship is one of the most practical ways you can honor God through this project.

Why Alignment Matters

Imagine a shopping cart with one wheel turned sideways. You push it forward, but it keeps drifting to the right. You're spending energy fighting the cart instead of moving forward. Your mousetrap car faces the exact same problem when its components are out of alignment.

When your axles aren't perfectly straight, or your wheels aren't sitting flush and parallel to each other, every rotation creates extra friction. That friction steals energy — energy that was supposed to carry your car across the floor. The result is a car that travels less distance, moves slower, or veers off course instead of going straight.

Alignment is essentially the relationship between components. When that relationship is right, energy flows efficiently through the system. When it's off, you fight the design at every step.

data.html:
What Quality Looks Like in Your Car

Quality isn't just about appearance — it's about how reliably each component does its job. In engineering, quality is measured against design specifications: did this part meet the requirements? In your mousetrap car, that means asking whether each component performs its intended function without introducing problems.

Common Quality Issues to Look For

  • Bent axles: Even a slight bend causes the wheel to wobble with every rotation, generating friction and wasting energy. Roll the axle on a flat surface — a bent axle will bounce or roll unevenly.
  • Rough or uneven wheel edges: Burrs or rough spots on the wheel rim create bumpy contact with the ground, reducing smooth rolling motion.
  • Loose wheel fit: A wheel that wobbles side-to-side on its axle wastes energy and can eventually fall off during a run.
  • Uneven string winding: If your drive string isn't wound evenly on the axle, it can bunch up, causing jerky motion or premature release of energy.
  • Off-center wheel mounting: A wheel that isn't centered on the axle creates a wobbly rotation — like a tire that's out of balance on a car.

The Roll Test: Before mounting your axles, lay them on a flat, hard surface and roll them slowly. If the axle wobbles, bounces, or doesn't roll in a straight line, it's bent. A straight axle rolls smoothly and stays in contact with the surface the whole time. Fix or replace bent axles before assembly — it's much harder to correct after the car is built.

Thinking at Multiple Scales

Here's where multiscale modeling becomes a powerful engineering mindset. Your mousetrap car's performance at the macro scale — how far it travels — is directly shaped by what's happening at a much smaller scale: the roughness of a wheel edge, the tiny wobble in an axle, the microscopic friction between a string and an axle.

Engineers who think at multiple scales catch problems that others miss. You might look at your car and think it looks fine. But zoom in — run your finger along the wheel edge. Feel for roughness. Check whether the axle spins freely in its bearing or drags slightly. Small imperfections at the micro scale add up to big performance losses at the macro scale.

This is why professional engineers use tolerances — defined allowable ranges of variation. A tolerance tells you how much a dimension can deviate from the design spec and still be acceptable. In your car, you're working by feel and observation, but the principle is the same: small deviations matter.

data.html:
Practical Techniques for Improving Alignment and Quality

Knowing what to look for is only half the job. Here's how to actually fix the problems you find.

Straightening and Checking Axles

If your axle is slightly bent, you may be able to carefully straighten it by rolling it between two flat, hard surfaces with gentle pressure. If it's severely bent, replace it. A straight axle is non-negotiable for good performance.

Smoothing Wheel Edges

Use fine-grit sandpaper to lightly sand any rough spots on your wheel edges. The goal is a smooth, consistent surface that makes even contact with the ground. Don't over-sand — you just want to remove burrs and rough patches, not reshape the wheel.

Securing Wheels Properly

When mounting wheels to axles, make sure the wheel sits centered and perpendicular (at a 90° angle) to the axle. If you're using glue, let it cure fully before testing. If you're using a mechanical fastener, check that it's snug but not overtightened in a way that restricts rotation.

Checking Parallel Alignment

Set your car on a flat surface and sight down from above. Your front axle and rear axle should be parallel to each other. If they're angled differently, your car will curve to one side. Adjust mounting positions carefully until both axles are aligned.

Even String Winding

Wind your drive string onto the axle slowly and deliberately, keeping each wrap tight and next to the previous one. Uneven winding causes energy release to be jerky and unpredictable.

Don't skip the inspection step. One of the most common mistakes in the mousetrap car build is going straight from assembly to testing without checking alignment and quality. Testing a misaligned car tells you very little useful information — it's hard to know if a poor run is due to your design or a fixable quality issue. Always inspect and correct before you test.

Objectives, Constraints, and Variables in Performance

Every engineering problem has three key elements working together. Your objective is what you're trying to achieve — in this case, maximum distance and straight-line travel. Your constraints are the rules you must follow — the size of your car, the materials you're allowed to use, the single mousetrap as your only power source. Your variables are the things you can adjust — axle placement, wheel size, string length, and of course, alignment and quality of each component.

When you improve alignment and quality, you're optimizing your variables to better achieve your objective within your constraints. That's the core logic of engineering design. Every tweak you make to straighten an axle or smooth a wheel edge is a deliberate engineering decision, not just tinkering.

data.title: Going Deeper: How Surface Roughness Affects Friction (Optional)
data.html:
At a microscopic level, no surface is perfectly smooth — even surfaces that look smooth to the naked eye have tiny peaks and valleys called asperities. When two surfaces slide against each other, these microscopic features interlock and resist motion. That resistance is friction.

Engineers who design high-performance systems — like race car wheel bearings or precision robotic joints — use surface finish measurements (often called Ra values, for average roughness) to specify exactly how smooth a surface must be. The smoother the surface, the less friction, and the more efficiently energy is transferred through the system.

In your mousetrap car, you're doing a simplified version of the same thing when you sand your wheel edges or make sure your axle spins freely. You're reducing surface roughness to minimize friction — improving performance from the microscale up.

Bringing It All Together

God's creation is our model. Every planet stays in its orbit. Every cell in your body performs its specific function with extraordinary reliability. That kind of performance doesn't happen by accident — it's the result of perfect design, perfect alignment, and perfect quality at every scale.

Your mousetrap car is your opportunity to pursue that same standard. Not because your car has to be perfect, but because the effort you put into aligning your components and improving their quality reflects genuine care — for your work, for your teammates, and for the calling God has placed on you as a creator and engineer.

Check your axles. Smooth your wheels. Align your components carefully. Then test — and see how much farther careful craftsmanship takes you.
